results.result: The manuscript establishes the biological context for studying allopolyploidization in Capsella bursa-pastoris, describing it as a natural allotetraploid that originated ~100,000 years ago from C. orientalis (self-compatible) and C. grandiflora (self-incompatible) progenitors. Prior work has characterized C. bursa-pastoris as having well-retained subgenomes with moderate expression bias and tissue-specific gene expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C19, C103-C104 provide background information supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Douglas et al., 2015; Hurka et al., 2012; Bachmann et al., 2019; Kryvokhyzha et al., 2019a; Neuffer and Paetsch, 2013). These claims establish the scientific context and are appropriately attributed to published work.

results.result: Natural C. bursa-pastoris exhibits a selfing syndrome with smaller floral organs, fewer pollen grains, and shorter stems compared to resynthesized allotetraploids, which more closely resemble the outcrossing parent C. grandiflora. This suggests the selfing syndrome evolved after allopolyploidization rather than arising immediately from dominance of C. orientalis alleles.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C29 are supported by statistical analyses (ANOVA, Tukey's HSD tests) with appropriate sample sizes (n=28-171 depending on trait) and significant p-values (<0.001). The morphological measurements in Figure 2a-k show clear differences between groups. The inference in C86 that the selfing syndrome evolved post-allopolyploidization is logically supported by the observation that resynthesized allotetraploids lack these traits despite having C. orientalis as a parent.

results.result: Resynthesized allotetraploids show reduced pollen viability and increased abnormal seed production compared to natural C. bursa-pastoris and diploid parents, suggesting that improved meiotic behavior evolved in natural allotetraploids over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C34 are supported by statistical analyses (GLM with quasi-binomial distribution, Tukey's HSD tests) showing significant differences (p<0.001) between groups. The data show resynthesized allotetraploids have 69.6-77.5% normal seeds versus 99.6% in natural Cbp. Claims C87-C89 provide mechanistic context from prior literature, though C87 is speculative about the mechanism in this system.

results.result: RNA-sequencing analysis reveals that resynthesized allotetraploids have gene expression patterns intermediate between diploid parents, while natural C. bursa-pastoris shows divergence from resynthesized allotetraploids, indicating long-term evolutionary changes in gene expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 are supported by MDS analysis of RNA-seq data from 60 samples (5 groups × 6 lines × 2 tissues). Claims C99-C101 describe the experimental design and data quality metrics (average 38.4-70.0 million mapped reads). The phasing analysis (C37) shows 44.7-53.7% of reads could be assigned to homoeologs. The MDS plots in Figure 3 visually support the intermediate positioning of resynthesized allotetraploids and divergence of natural Cbp.

results.result: Differential expression analysis reveals no significant DEGs between the two resynthesized allotetraploid groups, but 311-2888 DEGs in other comparisons. Most DEGs in allotetraploids are up-regulated compared to diploid parents, with the proportion of down-regulated DEGs increasing in natural allotetraploids.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 are supported by differential expression analysis using appropriate statistical methods (edgeR, FC>2, FDR<0.05) on 21,937 genes in flowers and 18,999 genes in leaves. The lack of DEGs between Sd and Sh groups (C40) is notable and suggests reproducible effects. Claim C46 reports GO enrichment analysis results, though only one term (proteolysis) remained significant after multiple testing correction, limiting biological interpretation.

results.result: Expression level dominance (ELD) doubled in natural allotetraploids (10.2%) compared to resynthesized allotetraploids (5.5%), with 40% of natural ELD cases already present in resynthesized allotetraploids. The direction of ELD shifted toward the self-fertilizing parent (C. orientalis) in natural allotetraploids, particularly in flowers.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C54 are supported by gene expression classification analysis using appropriate statistical thresholds (FC>2, FDR<0.05). The Venn diagram analysis (Figure 4c) shows 63.3-72.2% of shared ELD retained in natural allotetraploids, supporting the inference of short-term deterministic mechanisms (C90). However, 56.6-60.8% of ELD in natural allotetraploids is Cbp-specific, supporting long-term evolution (C91). The shift from predominantly Cg-ELD in resynthesized to more Co-ELD in natural allotetraploids (C51-C54) is well-documented. Claim C92 about intergenomic interactions is inferential but reasonably supported by the repeatability of ELD patterns.

results.result: Transgressive expression (TRE) is virtually absent in resynthesized allotetraploids (<5 genes) but present in ~1.3% of genes in natural C. bursa-pastoris, indicating that transcriptional novelties arise primarily during long-term evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by gene expression classification data shown in Figure 4. The stark contrast between resynthesized (<5 genes) and natural allotetraploids (~1.3% or ~280 genes) is clear. Claim C93 appropriately cites prior work (Flagel and Wendel, 2010; Yoo et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016b) showing similar patterns in other systems, strengthening the conclusion.

results.result: Resynthesized allotetraploids show striking variation in homoeolog expression bias (HEB) among chromosomes and individuals, with homoeologous synapsis being the primary source. HMM analysis reveals that only 39 of 96 chromosome quartets showed no sign of homoeologous synapsis, and the estimated copy number of homoeologs explains 48.4-46.8% of HEB variance.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C67 are supported by comprehensive HEB analysis on 18,255 genes in flowers and 15,581 genes in leaves. The average HEB values (C57-C58) show no strong bias, but Levene's test (C59, p<0.001) confirms greater variation in resynthesized allotetraploids. The HMM segmentation analysis (C64-C66) provides quantitative evidence for homoeologous synapsis, with an average of 0.833±0.097 breakpoints per chromosome quartet and 31.0% of genes having unbalanced homoeolog numbers. The GLM analysis (C67, p<0.001) demonstrates that copy number explains substantial HEB variance. The distribution patterns in Figure 5 with peaks at 0, 0.25, 0.75, and 1 (C61) are consistent with segregation of homoeologous chromosomes.

results.result: Natural C. bursa-pastoris shows more uniform HEB distribution than resynthesized allotetraploids, though some candidate segments with unbalanced homoeolog content are shared within populations, suggesting that occasional homoeologous synapsis may still contribute to genetic variation despite improved preferential synapsis.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by HEB distribution analysis (Figure 5), showing more uniform patterns in natural Cbp. However, claims C69, C83, C94-C95, C97-C98 are more speculative. The authors acknowledge limitations in detecting smaller segments with RNA-seq data alone (low resolution, technical variation). The HMM segmentation in natural Cbp (Figure 6) identifies candidate segments, but without genomic DNA sequencing or cytological validation, it's uncertain whether these represent true homoeologous exchanges, secondary introgression, or technical artifacts. The inference that preferential synapsis improved rapidly (C94) or that selection favored balanced homoeolog numbers (C95) is logical but not directly tested. Claims C97-C98 about the potential importance of low-frequency homoeologous synapsis are reasonable speculation but lack direct evidence.

results.result: Most resynthesized allotetraploids show lower levels of homoeolog-specific expression loss (average 1.0% in natural Cbp) than natural allotetraploids, but three outlier individuals (Sd-6-4, Sd-8-5, Sh-5-5) show extremely high expression loss restricted to chromosome 3, likely caused by homoeologous chromosome segregation and recombination.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by homoeolog expression loss analysis (Figure 7) using genes with CPM>5 in all diploid individuals but CPM<0.5 in allotetraploids. The three outliers show dramatically elevated expression loss. Claim C73 is a reasonable inference supported by the observation that extreme HEB in these individuals is restricted to chromosome 3 (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplements 3-6), consistent with loss or replacement of an entire chromosome or large chromosomal segment.

results.result: In resynthesized allotetraploids, ELD is primarily achieved through expression changes in the EL-recessive homoeolog while the EL-dominant homoeolog remains relatively unchanged, consistent with intergenomic regulatory interactions. In natural allotetraploids, both homoeologs show expression changes, particularly for Cbp-specific ELD and TRE.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by homoeolog expression change analysis (Figure 8). The pattern in resynthesized allotetraploids (C74) fits the third scenario of intergenomic cis-trans interactions, where EL-recessive homoeologs show larger expression changes while EL-dominant homoeologs remain near zero. The different pattern in Cbp-specific ELD (C75) and TRE (C76), where both homoeologs change expression, suggests different mechanisms operate during long-term evolution. The analysis appropriately considers alternative mechanisms (homoeologous synapsis, random effects, regulatory interactions) and uses the data to distinguish among them.

results.result: Both short-term and long-term mechanisms contributed to transcriptomic and phenotypic changes in natural allotetraploids, but initial gene expression changes were largely reshaped during long-term evolution, leading to further morphological changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing results from phenotypic, differential expression, ELD, TRE, and HEB analyses. The evidence shows that while ~40% of ELD is shared between resynthesized and natural allotetraploids (short-term), ~60% is Cbp-specific (long-term). TRE is almost entirely absent in resynthesized allotetraploids but present in natural ones. The selfing syndrome is absent in resynthesized allotetraploids despite having the self-compatible parent. These multiple lines of evidence collectively support the two-phase model of allopolyploid evolution.

results.result: Transposable elements (TEs) may not function as a strong mutagenic mechanism of HEB variation but could affect selection on HEB variation as a form of genetic load.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 is speculative and not directly tested in this study. The authors discuss TE content as a potential mechanism for HEB based on prior literature (Woodhouse et al., 2014) but do not analyze TE content or distribution in their samples. The claim is presented as speculation in the discussion to reconcile their findings with prior observations, but lacks direct supporting evidence from this work.

results.result: The breakdown of self-incompatibility in allotetraploid Capsella can directly result from hybridizing with the self-fertilizing species.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by citations to Bachmann et al., 2021 and Duan et al., 2023. This provides context for understanding the self-compatibility of the resynthesized allotetraploids used in this study.

results.result: Natural C. bursa-pastoris exhibits a selfing syndrome with smaller floral organs, fewer pollen grains, and higher seed production compared to resynthesized allotetraploids. The authors conclude this selfing syndrome evolved after allopolyploidization rather than arising immediately from hybridization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, stating 'The phenotypic data indicate that the selfing syndrome of C. bursa-pastoris likely evolved after the initial allopolyploidization event' and describing the results as 'compelling.' The editor notes the authors 'marshal compelling evidence' to distinguish roles of hybridization, WGD, and subsequent evolution in selfing syndrome phenotypes.

results.result: Natural allotetraploids recovered pollen and seed viability to levels similar to diploid parents, while resynthesized allotetraploids showed significantly reduced viability. The authors suggest this recovery was achieved through improved meiotic behaviors during long-term evolution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state 'pollen and seed viability recovered following the allopolyploidization event' and describe the results as 'compelling.' One reviewer notes the phenotypic data are strong but suggests minor methodological improvements (using linear mixed models rather than ANOVA).

results.result: Overall gene expression patterns show resynthesized allotetraploids are intermediate between diploid parents, while natural C. bursa-pastoris shows distinct expression patterns reflecting long-term evolution. Most differentially expressed genes are up-regulated in allotetraploids compared to diploid progenitors.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall contribution, with one stating the study provides 'new insights into the mechanisms driving evolution in allopolyploids' and praising 'the detailed examination of different mechanisms driving gene expression variation.' The editor confirms the authors use 'RNA sequencing...to distinguish the roles of hybridization, whole genome duplication, and subsequent evolution...in gene expression.'

results.result: Expression level dominance (ELD) doubled in natural allotetraploids (10.2%) compared to resynthesized ones (5.5%). About 40% of ELD cases in natural allotetraploids were already present in resynthesized lines, suggesting short-term deterministic mechanisms, while over 50% are Cbp-specific, indicating long-term evolutionary changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as demonstrating both short- and long-term contributions to expression evolution. One reviewer notes the study 'effectively separat[es] the contributions of hybridization, WGD, and evolution over time' and describes it as 'an interesting and valuable contribution to the field's understanding of how expression evolves in interaction with hybridization and polyploidy.'

results.result: Transgressive expression (TRE) was nearly absent in resynthesized allotetraploids but present in about 1.3% of genes in natural C. bursa-pastoris, indicating transcriptional novelties arose mainly during long-term evolution rather than immediately upon allopolyploidization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the overall pattern showing long-term evolutionary changes. One reviewer explicitly states the study demonstrates 'a combination of short and long-term changes to gene expression' and the manuscript is 'thorough and provides lots of new insights.'

results.result: Homeolog expression bias (HEB) showed striking variation among chromosomes and individuals in resynthesized allotetraploids, with large genomic segments showing sudden changes in HEB. Homoeologous synapsis was identified as the primary source of this variation, with 31% of genes estimated to have unbalanced homoeolog copy numbers. In contrast, natural C. bursa-pastoris showed more uniform HEB distributions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as 'intriguing evidence that segregation can be an important source of variation in allopolyploids.' One reviewer notes this is a valuable contribution, though acknowledges it was 'limited by the difficulty of inferring homeologous recombination breakpoints with RNAseq data' and suggests this as a future direction.

results.result: Some candidate genomic segments with unbalanced homoeolog content were found in natural C. bursa-pastoris populations, suggesting occasional homoeologous synapsis may still occur and provide genetic variation even after 100,000 years. The authors infer that preferential synapsis was rapidly improved or balanced homoeolog numbers were strongly selected.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this as 'intriguing evidence' but note significant limitations. One reviewer states the findings were 'limited by the difficulty of inferring homeologous recombination breakpoints with RNAseq data because of the scale of recombination in wild populations' and suggests 'identifying such breakpoints will be an interesting direction for this and other allopolyploid systems' in the future.

results.result: For ELD in resynthesized allotetraploids, expression changes primarily occurred in the recessive homoeolog while the dominant homoeolog remained stable, consistent with intergenomic regulatory interactions. In Cbp-specific ELD, both homoeologs showed expression changes, and for TRE both homoeologs changed in the same direction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these mechanistic findings as part of the 'detailed examination of different mechanisms driving gene expression variation' that one reviewer 'especially appreciated.' The findings contribute to understanding how expression evolves in allopolyploids.

results.result: GO enrichment analysis revealed only one significantly overrepresented term (proteolysis) in genes differentially expressed between resynthesized and natural allotetraploids in leaves after multiple testing correction.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly suggests this analysis should be expanded, stating 'Future research, or the current study, could also valuably explore what kinds of genes experienced what forms of expression evolution. A brief description of GO terms frequently represented in genes which showed strong patterns of expression evolution might be suggestive of which selective pressures led to the changes.' This indicates the current GO analysis is viewed as insufficient.

results.result: Homoeolog-specific expression loss was generally low (1.0% in natural Cbp), but three resynthesized individuals showed extremely high levels restricted to chromosome 3, likely caused by homoeologous chromosome segregation and recombination.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall evidence for homoeologous synapsis effects. The extreme cases in three individuals support the interpretation of ongoing chromosomal instability in resynthesized allotetraploids.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C70-C73 regarding homoeolog expression loss in three outlier individuals and the inference of chromosome 3 loss/replacement. Both evaluations find these claims supported by the data.

Strong agreement on claims C57-C67, C81-C82 regarding HEB analysis and homoeologous synapsis evidence. Both find the findings supported, though peer reviewers note the analysis was 'limited by the difficulty of inferring homeologous recombination breakpoints with RNAseq data.' OpenEval does not include C68 in this result, which peer reviewers address separately.

Strong agreement on claims C47-C54, C80, C90-C91 regarding ELD patterns and the two-phase model. Both evaluations find these claims supported and view them as effectively demonstrating short- and long-term contributions to expression evolution.

Agreement on claims C74-C76 regarding homoeolog expression changes and mechanistic interpretations. Both find these claims supported as part of understanding mechanisms driving gene expression variation in allopolyploids. OpenEval does not include C92 in this result.

Agreement on claims C55-C56, C93 regarding TRE patterns. Both find these claims supported as demonstrating long-term evolutionary changes. OpenEval includes C93 (literature context), while peer review includes C78 (which OpenEval addresses in R6).

Agreement on uncertainty regarding claims C69, C83, C94-C95, C97 about homoeologous synapsis evolution and selection. Both evaluations acknowledge these as speculative with significant limitations due to RNA-seq resolution constraints. OpenEval also includes C98 as speculative, while peer review does not explicitly address it.

Strong agreement on claims C20-C29, C77, C86 regarding selfing syndrome phenotypes evolving post-allopolyploidization. Both find these claims supported and compelling. Peer review also includes seed viability claims (C30-C34) in this result, which OpenEval addresses separately in R3.

Agreement on claims C30-C34, C77, C87 regarding seed viability recovery. Both find these claims supported. Peer reviewers suggest minor methodological improvements (linear mixed models vs ANOVA). OpenEval includes C88-C89 (mechanistic context), which peer review does not explicitly address.

Agreement on claims C40-C45 regarding differential expression analysis. Both find these claims supported as part of the overall contribution to understanding expression evolution. OpenEval also addresses C46 (GO enrichment) in this result, which peer review addresses separately in R9.

Partial overlap on claims C35-C36, C38-C39 regarding MDS analysis and RNA-seq experimental design. Both find these claims supported. OpenEval includes additional claims about phasing analysis (C37) and data quality metrics (C99-C101) not explicitly addressed by peer reviewers.

Disagreement on claim C46 regarding GO enrichment analysis. OpenEval finds it supported but notes limited biological interpretation (only one significant term after correction). Peer reviewers view it as uncertain/insufficient and suggest expanding the analysis to explore what kinds of genes experienced different forms of expression evolution.
